title: 睡眠与记忆
sub: 讲座 / 讲话 Lecture · 博浩原创真题风格语料

data.text:
Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about why sleep is so important for learning.
For a long time, people treated sleep as wasted time, but research has completely changed that view.
Studies show that while we sleep, the brain replays the information we learned during the day and moves it into long-term memory.
This process is especially active during deep sleep and during the dreaming stage called REM sleep.
In one experiment, students who slept for eight hours after studying remembered about twenty percent more than those who stayed awake.
The timing also matters: reviewing material shortly before sleep seems to help it stick.
So if you have an important exam, the best advice is simple.
Do not stay up all night memorising. Instead, study during the day, get a full night's sleep, and review again the next morning.
Your brain will do the rest of the work while you rest.

title: 如何高效做课堂笔记
sub: 讲座 / 讲话 Lecture · 博浩原创真题风格语料

data.text:
Hello everyone. Today's topic is note-taking, a skill that most students never actually learn.
Many students try to write down every word the teacher says, but that is both tiring and ineffective.
Research shows that people remember material better when they process it while writing.
A better method is to listen first, then write down key ideas in your own words.
Leave a wide margin on each page so you can add questions and comments later.
You should also review your notes within twenty-four hours, when the memory is still fresh.
Colour can help: use one colour for definitions and another for examples.
But do not spend too much time decorating your notes, because the purpose is understanding, not art.
Finally, compare notes with a classmate once a week to catch anything you missed.
If you follow these steps, your notes will become a real learning tool instead of a boring copy of the textbook.

For a long time, people treated sleep as wasted time, but research has completely changed that view.

title: 睡前使用手机的危害

Good evening, everyone. Tonight I want to discuss a habit that quietly harms millions of people: using phones in bed.
You may have noticed that after scrolling through your phone, you feel wide awake instead of sleepy.
There are two main reasons for this.
First, the blue light from the screen tricks your brain into thinking it is still daytime.
Second, the content itself is exciting, whether it is news, games or messages, and it keeps your mind racing.
Together, these effects delay the release of melatonin, the hormone that helps you fall asleep.

Good evening, everyone. Tonight I want to discuss a habit that quietly harms millions of people: using phones in bed.
You may have noticed that after scrolling through your phone, you feel wide awake instead of sleepy.
There are two main reasons for this.
First, the blue light from the screen tricks your brain into thinking it is still daytime.
Second, the content itself is exciting, whether it is news, games or messages, and it keeps your mind racing.
Together, these effects delay the release of melatonin, the hormone that helps you fall asleep.
Over time, this can lead to a vicious circle of late nights and tired mornings.
The solution is surprisingly simple.
Set a rule for yourself: no screens for thirty minutes before bedtime.
Leave your phone charging outside the bedroom, and use an ordinary alarm clock instead.
At first it will feel strange, but within a week, most people fall asleep faster and wake up feeling more rested.

Your brain will do the rest of the work while you rest.

Explaining is the fastest way to find out whether you truly understand the research.

You may have noticed that after scrolling through your phone, you feel wide awake instead of sleepy.

Set a rule for yourself: no screens for thirty minutes before bedtime.

You may have noticed that after scrolling through your phone, you feel wide awake instead of sleepy.

Set a rule for yourself: no screens for thirty minutes before bedtime.
Leave your phone charging outside the bedroom, and use an ordinary alarm clock instead.

You may have noticed that after scrolling through your phone, you feel wide awake instead of sleepy.

First, the blue light from the screen tricks your brain into thinking it is still daytime.

Set a rule for yourself: no screens for thirty minutes before bedtime.
Leave your phone charging outside the bedroom, and use an ordinary alarm clock instead.

Hello, everyone. Many learners ask me why their English is not improving despite years of study.
The most common reason is that they only receive English and never produce it.
Input, such as listening and reading, builds your vocabulary and sense of the language.
But output, such as speaking and writing, is what turns that knowledge into a skill.
Think of it like learning to swim: you can watch videos about swimming all day, but you will not learn until you get into the water.
Here is a practical suggestion.
After each listening exercise, repeat the passage aloud and try to summarise it in your own words.
After each reading, write a short paragraph about the topic without looking at the text.
This forces your brain to retrieve the language you have stored, which strengthens your memory.
Aim for a balance: for every hour of input, spend at least fifteen minutes producing language.
Your speaking will feel difficult at first, but that difficulty is a sign of real progress.

We tend to think procrastinators are lazy, but research shows they are usually just avoiding unpleasant emotions.
A task feels boring, difficult or frightening, so the brain looks for immediate relief in entertainment.
The problem is that the relief is temporary, and the anxiety returns stronger than before.
One effective method is called the five-minute rule.
Tell yourself you will work on the task for just five minutes.

Another helpful trick is to break a large task into tiny pieces and reward yourself after each one.
Finally, forgive yourself for past procrastination, because guilt makes you more likely to avoid the task again.
Remember, the goal is not to feel motivated before you start; motivation often comes after action, not before it.

Good morning. Today I want to clear up some misunderstandings about plastic recycling.
Many people believe that throwing a plastic bottle into the recycling bin means it will definitely become a new bottle.
The reality is more complicated.
Only certain types of plastic can be recycled easily, and the process is expensive.
Recycled plastic is often lower in quality, so it cannot be used for the same products again.
As a result, much of what we put in recycling bins is still burned or buried.
Experts say the most effective solution is to reduce our use of plastic in the first place.
Carry a reusable bottle, refuse single-use packaging, and choose products with less plastic.
When you do use plastic, make sure it is clean and dry before recycling, because dirty items contaminate whole batches.
Check the number on the bottom of the container to see whether it is actually recyclable in your area.
Remember the order that really works: reduce first, reuse second, and recycle only as a last step.

Good evening, everyone. Tonight I want to discuss a habit that quietly harms millions of people: using phones in bed.
You may have noticed that after scrolling through your phone, you feel wide awake instead of sleepy.
There are two main reasons for this.
First, the blue light from the screen tricks your brain into thinking it is still daytime.
Second, the content itself is exciting, whether it is news, games or messages, and it keeps your mind racing.
Together, these effects delay the release of melatonin, the hormone that helps you fall asleep.
Over time, this can lead to a vicious circle of late nights and tired mornings.
The solution is surprisingly simple.
Set a rule for yourself: no screens for thirty minutes before bedtime.
Leave your phone charging outside the bedroom, and use an ordinary alarm clock instead.
At first it will feel strange, but within a week, most people fall asleep faster and wake up feeling more rested.

So if you have an important exam, the best advice is simple.
Do not stay up all night memorising. Instead, study during the day, get a full night's sleep, and review again the next morning.
Your brain will do the rest of the work while you rest.

Caffeine is found in coffee, tea, chocolate and many soft drinks.
In small amounts, it can make you more alert, improve your mood and help you concentrate.

However, caffeine has a downside that is often ignored.
It takes several hours for its effects to disappear, and it can stay in your body much longer.
If you drink coffee in the afternoon, it may still be interfering with your sleep at night.
Too much caffeine can also make you anxious and give you headaches when you stop.
Experts suggest that adults limit themselves to about four hundred milligrams a day, which is roughly four small cups of coffee.

title: 如何阅读学术论文
sub: 讲座 / 讲话 Lecture · 博浩原创真题风格语料

data.text:
Good morning, everyone. Reading academic papers can feel overwhelming, but there is a smarter way to do it.
Most students make the mistake of reading a paper from beginning to end like a novel.
Instead, start with the abstract, which summarises the whole study in one paragraph.
Then read the conclusion to learn what the authors found and why it matters.
Only after that should you look at the introduction and the methods.
When you reach the results section, focus on the figures and tables first, because they tell the main story.
Keep a question in your mind as you read: what is the single most important finding?
If a section is too technical, do not get stuck; mark it and move on, then come back later.
Finally, write two or three sentences in your own words explaining the paper to a classmate.
Explaining is the fastest way to find out whether you truly understand the research.

title: 时间管理中的二八法则
sub: 讲座 / 讲话 Lecture · 博浩原创真题风格语料

data.text:
Welcome, everyone. Today I want to introduce a simple idea that can transform how you spend your time.
It is called the 80/20 rule, and it says that roughly eighty percent of your results come from twenty percent of your efforts.
In studying, this means a small number of key topics usually account for most of the marks in an exam.
Yet many students spend equal time on every chapter, including the ones that rarely appear.
Start by identifying the topics that have the greatest impact on your grades.
Give those topics most of your attention, and deal with the rest later.
The same logic applies to daily tasks: two or three important tasks matter far more than ten small ones.
Each morning, write down the three tasks that would make today a success, and do them first.
Avoid the trap of feeling busy while actually doing unimportant work.
Remember, being busy is not the same as being productive.
